sec.title: Background
sec.p: In the setting of curative treatment of breast carcinoma, radiotherapy is usually administered after surgery (adjuvant radiotherapy).
We intend to evaluate the impact of delivering radiation therapy prior to surgical intervention in the treatment of these patients.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: The NEO-HYPORT trial is designed as a randomised, controlled, parallel group, open-label, single-centre, superiority trial comparing neoadjuvant and adjuvant radiotherapy after neoadjuvant chemotherapy. The primary endpoint is 3-year disease-free survival. A secondary randomisation will evaluate two hypofractionated radiotherapy schedules (40 Gy / 15 fractions / 3 weeks vs 26 Gy / 5 fractions / 1 week) in the two settings.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Conventionally radiation therapy is delivered following surgery as adjuvant radiation therapy. The reasons for the same have been manifold including the hypothesis that surgical wound healing following radiation therapy may be delayed. Various biological arguments and outcomes from the utilisation of neoadjuvant radiation in other tumour sites suggest that neoadjuvant radiation may provide superior disease control as compared to adjuvant radiation therapy. Emerging evidence on wound healing safety following radiotherapy to the breast is also reported. The NEO-HYPORT trial will provide high-quality evidence about the efficacy of neoadjuvant radiotherapy and establish the safety of ultra hypofractionated radiotherapy in this setting.
Keywords: Breast cancer, Hypofractionated radiotherapy, Neoadjuvant radiotherapy

sec.title: Background and rationale {6a}
sec.p: Breast cancer is the most common cancer affecting humans globally with an estimated 2.3 million new cases being diagnosed worldwide annually [1]. Radiotherapy, locally targeted to the breast/chest wall and or regional lymph nodes, is a core component of multi-disciplinary management of breast cancer. Interestingly, EBCTCG meta-analyses have demonstrated that use of adjuvant radiotherapy resulted in a clinically meaningful and statistically significant improvement in breast cancer-specific survival after both breast conservation and mastectomy [2, 3]. This therefore suggests a systemic benefit (survival) associated with the advantage of local control, with the use of a local therapy. The current paradigm for combination of radiotherapy is to use it after surgery and this form of radiotherapy has been referred to as post-operative or adjuvant radiotherapy (ART).

An alternative method to administer radiotherapy is to administer it before surgery—also known as pre-operative or neoadjuvant radiotherapy (NART). Major theoretical advantages of NART include the improved pathological complete response rates, greater downstaging of the tumour, treatment of the tumour in situ which is arguably better vascularised and possibly having an immunogenic potential as well as potential for better reconstruction [4]. Disadvantages include a higher potential for wound complications due to the use of radiotherapy.

sec.title: Review of status of research and development in the subject
sec.p: NART is not a new concept and the Stockholm Breast cancer trial investigated this approach in patients with operable breast cancer between 1971 and 1976 [5]. The randomised trial enrolled 960 patients with stage I–II disease who were operable upfront. Stage III patients were included only if they had stage designation by virtue of their tumour size. Patients undergoing NART (n = 365) mostly received radiotherapy to the entire breast, axillary apex, supraclavicular and internal mammary nodes and then modified radical mastectomy. Patients undergoing upfront surgery were also randomly allocated to receive either no further treatment (n = 323) or ART (n = 321). Evidence of tumour downstaging was obtained in the study as axillary nodal metastases were seen in 21% (65 of 365) patients receiving NART as compared to 37% (238 of 638) patients receiving ART. Survival outcomes favoured the NART arm as compared to either of the control arms. In the NART arm, 29 deaths (n = 316) whilst in the ART arm, 46 deaths (n = 323) were seen. Locoregional recurrence rates were similar but distant metastases rates favoured the NART arm over the ART arm. It is important to note that these results were obtained despite treatment using equipment and techniques that would be considered obsolete by modern standards. Additionally systemic therapy was not administered in the trial. Finally, there was a significant delay in surgery in the NART arm (the earliest surgery was done after 6 weeks after RT). These factors taken together may have resulted in reduced difference in the outcomes noted after longer follow-up despite a significant reduction in the risk of recurrence with radiotherapy (NART or ART) [6].

Improvements in systemic therapy have resulted in neoadjuvant systemic therapy being integrated into the management paradigm of locally advanced breast cancers. Additionally, patients with triple negative and HER2neu enriched tumours are also preferentially treated with systemic therapy prior to surgery. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy has also been used to allow breast conservation in patients with an unfavourable tumour to breast ratio [4].

NART has been combined with neoadjuvant chemotherapy in several studies. Calais et al. reported outcomes of a group of patients with locally advanced breast cancers treated with neoadjuvant anthracycline-based chemotherapy followed by mastectomy or conservative treatment with radiation therapy alone or NART [7]. Breast conservation was feasible in 77 of 158 patients in the study and 32 received radiotherapy alone. Five-year overall survival was 73.2% and was higher in patients with response to systemic therapy. Coelho et al. reported the use of NART to a dose of 50 Gy in 25 fractions in 57 patients who had poor or no response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy [8]. In their retrospective series, 98.2% received anthracycline-based chemotherapy and 75.4% had a downstaging followed by further mastectomy. Patients undergoing mastectomy had a median overall survival of 49 months. Another retrospective series by Lerouge et al. reported outcomes of 120 patients with locally advanced breast cancers treated with neoadjuvant anthracycline-based chemotherapy (4 cycles) followed by NART and an additional cycle of chemotherapy [9]. This was followed by mastectomy or breast conservation. It is noteworthy that tumour bed boost was delivered after surgery in patients undergoing breast conservation in these patients. Ten-year overall metastatic disease-free survival was 61%. Cosmetic results were also reported and were found to be satisfactory in 51.5% of patients undergoing breast conservation and RT. Interestingly in this study a group of patients underwent RT alone (n = 39) without any further surgery and in them the 10-year local recurrence rate was 13% indicating that durable local control can be obtained in a substantial proportion of patients with high doses of radiotherapy (in this group a boost of 25 Gy was delivered using brachytherapy). Matuschek et al. reported a study involving 315 patients treated with NART followed by anthracycline-based chemotherapy [10]. In this study, 29.2% of the patients had a pathological complete response and breast conservation was possible in 50.8% of the patients. Pathological complete response rate was identified to be a strong prognostic factor influencing outcomes in this study. Lin et al. reported the results of a multi-institutional series of patients with locally advanced breast cancers treated with NART following neoadjuvant chemotherapy [11]. Unlike the previous studies, this study had patients receiving stage and molecular subtype appropriate neoadjuvant systemic therapy along with NART. One hundred thirty-eight patients were treated and most received conventionally fractionated radiotherapy Pathological complete response was observed in 36.4% of the patients with a higher rate in HER2neu enriched and triple negative cancers. No grade 4 or 5 postoperative complications were observed and 15% of the patients had grade 3 post-operative complications. Overall survival was 95.3% at 3 years whilst locoregional recurrence-free survival at 3 years was 98.1%.

In patients with advanced cancers, the use of NART has been evaluated in several studies to assist breast reconstruction after mastectomy. Monrigal et al. reported the outcomes of immediate breast reconstruction after neoadjuvant chemotherapy, NART, and mastectomy in a series of 210 patients and showed that wound complications requiring further surgery were required in 23 patients. Implant complications were seen 23.6% in the long-term follow-up with a higher number of complications seen in patients undergoing retropectoral implant placement [12]. A similar experience was reported by Paillocher et al. in 111 patients in another retrospective series, where patients underwent mastectomy, autologous flap reconstruction after chemotherapy and NART. They reported a lower necrosis rate of 5.4% and encouraging 5-year disease-free survival of 93.2% [13]. Prospective data in this area also comes from the PRADA study which recruited 33 patients for preoperative radiotherapy followed by deep inferior epigastric perforator flap-based reconstruction [14]. Wound complication in the form of an open breast wound was seen in 12% of the patients. This study employed a moderately hypofractionated radiotherapy regimen of 40 Gy in 15 fractions over 3 weeks.

A phase III randomised trial has been initiated in Germany investigating NART after neoadjuvant chemotherapy in patients with carcinoma breast—NEORAD trial [15]. In this trial, 1826 patients will be randomised to receive moderately hypofractionated NART or ART with the primary endpoint being disease-free survival.

Over the past decade, the results of the FAST and FAST Forward trial have provided evidence for the use of an ultra-fractionated 1 week course of radiotherapy in breast cancer [16, 17]. In order to deliver a clinical trial with a true 1 week course of radiotherapy, we have also initiated the HYPORT Adjuvant trial where patients undergoing breast conservation can be treated with a simultaneous integrated boost [18]. Initial acute toxicity results from the HYPORT Adjuvant support the use of a 1 week regimen [19], though final outcome details are likely to be in 2029. However, by this period, results of the lymphatic substudy of the FAST Forward trial will also be available and if the primary endpoint of HYPORT Adjuvant is met, it is likely that the standard course of ART would be a 1 week, five fraction regimen of radiotherapy. Use of ultra-fractionated NART has been described by Thorpe et al. in a phase II trial, where patients with early operable breast disease were enrolled and received NART to a dose of 25 Gy in 5 fractions over 1 week [20]. Pathological complete responses were seen in 14% of the patients. Nine percent of the patients had an infected seroma and fibrosis in the postoperative period. In another study by Mulliez et al., NART was delivered in a dose of 25 Gy in 5 fractions to the whole breast along with a simultaneous integrated boost of 5 Gy to the gross disease [21]. Fourteen patients were treated in whom wound complications were documented in 5 patients. Cosmesis was good to excellent in 12 patients and all patients were disease free at 42 months. This study however recruited only patients with early-stage luminal disease. Metabolic responses to a 1 week course of radiotherapy with simultaneous integrated boost have also been reported by our group in a population of locally advanced and unresectable breast cancers [22]. In this prospective study, 30 patients were treated with whole breast radiotherapy to a dose of 26 Gy in five fractions along with a simultaneous integrated boost of 6 Gy to the gross disease. A complete metabolic response was documented in 17.4% of the patients, whilst 65.2% had a partial metabolic response.

sec.title: Importance/significance of the proposed project in the context of current status {6b}
sec.p: It can therefore be summarised that there is a need to investigate if NART results in an improved outcome among patients of breast cancer treated with neoadjuvant chemotherapy. Given the evidence regarding the activity and safety of NART, it is worthwhile to consider a randomised controlled trial. At the same time, it is important to evaluate a more resource-sparing ultra-fractionated radiotherapy course in this setting. The NEO-HYPORT trial is therefore being designed to meet these dual objectives.

sec.title: Research hypothesis
sec.p: Neoadjuvant radiotherapy results in improved outcomes as compared to adjuvant radiotherapy among patients of breast cancer. Additionally, there is no difference in late normal tissue effects when an ultra-hypofractionated radiotherapy regimen is used in the neoadjuvant setting vis a vis the adjuvant setting.

sec.title: Primary objective
sec.p: The primary objective of the study is to determine if neoadjuvant (preoperative) radiotherapy results in a better disease-free survival in patients of breast cancer receiving neoadjuvant radiotherapy as compared to adjuvant (postoperative) radiotherapy.

sec.title: Breast or chest wall induration
sec.p: The key secondary objective is to determine if there is a difference between the breast or chest wall induration between the two fractionation schedules being used in the trial.

sec.title: Additional cancer-related outcomes
sec.p: To determine if neoadjuvant radiotherapy results in better locoregional control, breast cancer-specific survival and overall survival as compared to adjuvant (postoperative) radiotherapy.

sec.title: Late normal tissue effects
sec.p: To determine if neoadjuvant radiotherapy results in worse late normal tissue effects as compared to adjuvant radiotherapy.

sec.title: Patient-reported outcomes
sec.p: To determine if neoadjuvant radiotherapy results in improved patient-reported outcomes as compared to adjuvant radiotherapy.

sec.title: Clinician-reported toxicity
sec.p: To compare if the neoadjuvant radiotherapy results in lower clinician-reported toxicity as compared to adjuvant radiotherapy.

list-item.p: Perforator substudy: This study will ascertain the patency of the perforators in patients undergoing neoadjuvant radiotherapy to determine the suitability of this procedure in patients undergoing chest wall perforator flaps for reconstruction.
Sentinel node substudy: This substudy will be planned to evaluate the detection rate of sentinel lymph nodes after neoadjuvant radiotherapy.

Pathological complete response rate: The substudy will ascertain the immediate efficacy of neoadjuvant radiotherapy by estimating the improvement in pathological complete response following neoadjuvant radiotherapy.
Surgical wound complication rates: This substudy will ascertain the safety of neoadjuvant radiotherapy in terms of surgical wound complications after neoadjuvant radiotherapy.

sec.title: Trial design {8}
sec.p: The NEO-HYPORT trial is designed as a randomised, controlled, open-label, single-centre, superiority trial with four parallel groups and a primary endpoint of 3-year disease-free survival after neoadjuvant treatment. Randomisation will be performed as permuted block randomisation with equal allocation.

sec.title: Study setting {9}
sec.p: The study is planned as a multicentric trial in tertiary cancer centres in India.

sec.title: Eligibility criteria {10}
sec.p: Patients must provide written informed consent before any study procedures occur (see Appendix I for sample patient information and informed consent form).

list-item.p: Age ≥ 18 years

Patients must have a pathological proof of an invasive epithelial breast malignancy at the treating institute. A core biopsy with adequate specimen quality is necessary for this. FNAC alone is not sufficient. Biopsies taken outside must have been reviewed for pathological confirmation and specimen adequacy at the treating institute. Patients with ductal and lobular cancers are eligible for the study.

Receptor status (Oestrogen receptor, Progesterone receptor and HER2 neu receptor) status should be documented. Patients can be enrolled with an equivocal HER2neu receptor report but in all such cases a confirmatory in situ hybridisation should be done to confirm the status prior to initiation of taxane-based chemotherapy.
ECOG performance status 0—2.

Clinical stage I—III disease as documented with adequate pretreatment staging. Adequate staging include either of the two following options:
Whole body 18-FDG PET CT (preferred)
Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the thorax and abdomen and a bone scan. Note that chest X-ray or USG abdomen are not acceptable substitutes.
Patients should have been planned for neoadjuvant chemotherapy as per institutional protocol.
Patients with tumour that is likely to be amenable for curative intent resection of the breast primary, following neoadjuvant therapy.

If the patient had nodal disease in the supraclavicular fossa (proven pathologically) or internal mammary nodes (proven radiologically or pathologically), then residual gross nodes should not be present in these regions post NACT.

sec.title: Exclusion criteria
sec.p: Presence of any of the following will exclude the patient from participation in the study:

list-item.p: Patients planned for therapeutic mammoplasty.
Patients planned for chest wall perforator flaps. This criteria will be re-evaluated after the data from the perforator substudy is available and has been reviewed by the DSMC.
Patients with non-epithelial malignant conditions of breast viz. Sarcomas, lymphomas and phyllodes breast tumours.
Patients with skin cancer affecting the breast.
Prior radiotherapy to the ipsilateral breast or chest wall or mediastinum.
Concurrent illness, including severe infection that may jeopardise the ability of the patient to undergo the procedures outlined in this protocol with reasonable safety
Serious medical or psychiatric conditions that might limit the ability of the patient to comply with the protocol.

sec.p: Patients enrolled for trials of investigational drugs should not be enrolled for this study.

sec.title: Screening criteria
sec.p: Written informed consent must be signed and dated by the subject, and signed and dated by the Investigator, prior to any study-specific screening investigations being performed.

sec.title: Registration
sec.p: Subjects must meet all of the inclusion criteria and none of the exclusion criteria to be eligible for this trial/study. There will be no exceptions made to these eligibility requirements at the time of registration. All enquiries about eligibility should be addressed by contacting the Clinical Trials Unit (CTU) prior to registration.

Subjects must be registered before starting study treatment. Requests for registration will only be accepted from authorised investigators at sites that have received ethics approval. Treatment should be planned to start within 28 days after registration. Registration should be done only after all screening assessments have been performed and the responsible investigator has both verified the subject’s eligibility, and signed the completed registration form.
Once the registration process has been completed, the subject will be assigned a subject study number, and written confirmation of registration will be provided to the site.

sec.title: Withdrawal criteria
sec.p: Participation in this study is voluntary; patients will be able to withdraw at any time. A patient may withdraw, or be withdrawn from study treatment for the following reasons:

list-item.p: Intercurrent illness which prevents further follow-up
Withdrawal of consent for treatment by patient
Any alterations in the patient’s condition which justifies the discontinuation in the investigator’s opinion

sec.p: If a patient or investigator decides to stop the study treatment then the patient’s health status will be periodically reviewed via continued study visits or phone contact, or from their general practitioner or medical records to allow collection of outcomes data.
Follow-up assessments including completion of the quality of life questionnaires should still be completed if the patient is willing.

In the event that a patient withdraws from the study entirely, the effective date of the notification will be the date on which their withdrawal is received by the study team. No information about the patient will be collected from that point in time onwards but any information collected prior to that date can be used and forms part of this study.

sec.title: Patient transfer
sec.p: As far as possible, the patient should remain under the care of the treating team. For patients moving from the area during follow-up, every effort should be made for the patient to be followed up at another participating trial centre and for this trial centre to take over responsibility for the patient. A copy of the patient Case Record Forms (CRF) will need to be provided to the new site after appropriate patient consent. Until the new centre agrees (in writing) to take over responsibility, the patient remains the responsibility of the original centre.

sec.title: Trial centre requirements
sec.p: Given the pragmatic design of this study, trial centres should be high volume centres treating at least 150 breast cancer patients annually as per the European Society of Breast Cancer Specialists (EUSOMA) guidelines 2013 [27] and should have facilities for surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy and a working pathology and radiology services. Ideally, there should be a dedicated multi-disciplinary team of surgeons, clinical/radiation oncologists, medical oncologists, pathologists and radiologists looking at breast cancer. The centre should report mammograms using the Breast Imaging Reporting and Data (BIRAD) system. Breast pathology services should have accredited services for evaluation of Oestrogen receptor, Progesterone receptor and Her2neu receptor status with immunohistochemistry.

For this study, breast cancer patients must be simulated through a volumetric imaging technique. Centres which have not been a part of the HYPORT Adjuvant trial should fulfil the trial quality assurance requirements as outlined in the Radiotherapy Quality Assurance (RTQA) document.

sec.title: Who will take informed consent {26a}
sec.p: Informed consent will be obtained by the investigators or designated study personnel of the trial.

sec.title: Additional consent provisions for collection and use of participant data and biological specimens {26b}
sec.p: Radiological images will be biobanked in CHAVI biobank after informed consent for CHAVI image biobanking. Tissue or other biospecimens will be biobanked after dedicated biobank consent.

sec.title: Intervention description {11a}
sec.p: Eligible patients will be randomised first to receive neoadjuvant versus adjuvant radiotherapy and then randomised between the 3 week and 1 week arm. Randomisation would be performed in equal proportions between the two arms. The rationale underlying the double randomisation is that it would allow us to compare the efficacy of neoadjuvant radiotherapy versus adjuvant radiotherapy. In addition, it will also allow us to determine if the postoperative complications, acute toxicity and late adverse effects due to a 1 week course of radiotherapy as compared to the 3 week course of treatment in the two settings.
The following will be the arms in the trial:

tr.td: Adjuvant external beam radiotherapy with 3 weeks of radiotherapy
Adjuvant external beam radiotherapy with 1 week of radiotherapy
Neoadjuvant external beam radiotherapy with 3 weeks of radiotherapy
Neoadjuvant external beam radiotherapy with 1 week of radiotherapy
Primary dose to breast (or chest wall if post mastectomy)

sec.title: Surgical assessment
sec.p: Patients will be reviewed by the surgery team prior to the start of any neoadjuvant radiotherapy and decisions for surgery (mastectomy or breast conservation) would be documented along with axillary staging. This assessment will be performed along with the baseline assessment post randomisation.

sec.title: Timing
sec.p: Patients receiving adjuvant radiotherapy should start radiotherapy within 12 weeks of surgery. Radiotherapy can be started as soon as wound healing is completed however. Ideally, radiotherapy should be started within 6 weeks of surgery.
In the neoadjuvant radiotherapy arm the radiotherapy should be started in 4–6 weeks after the last cycle of chemotherapy or after the recovery of post chemotherapy haematological toxicity.

sec.title: Equipment
sec.p: Megavoltage equipment capable of delivering static intensity modulation with a multileaf collimator or dynamic intensity modulation (using a multileaf collimator or tomotherapy) is required. For all patients, the allowed energies are 6–15 MV photons. For isocentric linear accelerators mounted on a C-arm gantry, the Source to Source Distance (SSD) should be 100 cm.

sec.title: Localisation, positioning and simulation
sec.p: Prior to radiotherapy, all patients will undergo CT simulation. All patients in study would undergo simulation in the supine position with arms abducted. Use of a breast board is allowed but should be prespecified at the time of commissioning. All CTs will be acquired with an interslice spacing of 2.5 mm or less.

Patients with left-sided breast cancers should ideally be treated with some form of breath hold radiotherapy technique to minimise the heart dose. If such an approach is desired in other centres, the same should be pre-specified in the trial commissioning and in the institutional process document.

sec.title: Boost in neoadjuvant radiotherapy arms
sec.p: In patients receiving neoadjuvant radiotherapy, the pretreatment PET CT, mammogram and post chemotherapy mammogram will be used to localise the residual gross disease for tumour bed boost. For patients receiving adjuvant radiotherapy, surgical clips placed at the tumour bed and the postoperative seroma will be used to localise the boost volume tumour bed boost.

sec.title: Boost in adjuvant radiotherapy arms
sec.p: The tumour bed clips have to be localised at the time of CT scan in patients treated after breast conservation. Tumour bed clips should be placed at the medial, lateral, superior and inferior aspect of the tumour bed, one placed dorsally at the pectoral fascia and one ventrally close to the suture line. An alternative technique of tumour bed boost like boost to the affected quadrant can be given if the tumour bed clips are not visualised.
The following patients will not undergo sequential boost after breast conservation surgery:

list-item.p: Where tumour bed clips are not placed or visualised.
Breast anatomy is such that it may require procedures like strapping to allow appropriate treatment planning.
When the cavity contour is felt to be complex and SIB planning does not achieve the set dose volume objectives.
Additional criteria as defined in the institutional process document.

sec.title: Selection of target volumes
sec.p: Neoadjuvant radiotherapy
The glandular tissue of the entire breast will be the primary target volume (CTVp_Breast). Additionally the residual gross disease will be delineated for a boost (GTVp).
Inclusion of regional nodal volume(s) in the target volume will follow the principles for adjuvant radiotherapy and will be as follows:

list-item.p:
Supraclavicular fossa (CTVn_L4): Will be included in patients who have axillary nodal involvement before the initiation of neoadjuvant chemotherapy. This would include any of the following:
Patients with clinical cN1-N3 disease (including supraclavicular fossa lymph node or internal mammary lymph node involvement). Cytological or pathological proof of malignancy should be obtained for supraclavicular lymph nodes. For internal mammary lymph nodes, radiological findings would be deemed sufficient and pathological proof is not required.
Patients presenting with involved ipsilateral axillary lymph nodes as documented by a fine-needle aspiration cytology or alternative biopsy techniques including pre-chemotherapy sentinel lymph node biopsy.
Patients with pathological lymph nodes documented on FDG PET CT and an additional imaging modality like mammogram or MRI of the breast.

Internal mammary nodes (CTVn_IMN): Will be included in patients who have any of the following:
Clinical, radiological or pathological evidence of involvement of the internal mammary lymph node at presentation.
cT4 or higher disease in the breast in any quadrant.
cN2 or higher axillary nodal disease status irrespective of primary tumour stage.
Clinical T1-T2 disease with N1 disease and tumour located partly or completely in the central or medial quadrant of the breast.

Axillary lymph nodes (CTVn_L1, CTVn_L2, CTVn_L3): These will be included only if the patients with axillary nodal involvement (cN1-N3) disease are not planned for axillary nodal dissection after NACT. In such a scenario, all three levels will be included.
Adjuvant radiotherapy

The primary clinical target volume will comprise the entire breast (CTVp_Breast) in patients who have undergone breast conservation surgery or the chest wall (CTVp_Chestwall) in those who have undergone a mastectomy. A tumour bed will also be delineated in patients undergoing breast conservation for tumour bed boost.
Regional nodal volumes will be included in the target volume in the following scenarios:

Supraclavicular fossa (CTVn_L4): Will be included in patients who have axillary nodal involvement before the initiation of neoadjuvant chemotherapy. This would include any of the following:
Patients with clinical cN1-N3 disease (including supraclavicular fossa lymph node or internal mammary lymph node involvement). Cytological or pathological proof of malignancy should be obtained for supraclavicular lymph nodes. For internal mammary lymph nodes, radiological findings would be deemed sufficient and pathological proof is not required.
Patients presenting with involved ipsilateral axillary lymph nodes as documented by a fine-needle aspiration cytology or alternative biopsy techniques including pre-chemotherapy sentinel lymph node biopsy.
Patients with pathological lymph nodes documented on FDG PET CT and an additional imaging modality like mammogram or MRI of the breast.

Internal mammary nodes (CTVn_IMN): Will be included in patients who have any of the following:
Clinical, radiological or pathological evidence of involvement of the internal mammary lymph node at presentation.
cT4 or higher disease in the breast in any quadrant.
cN2 or higher axillary nodal disease status irrespective of primary tumour stage.
Clinical T1-T2 disease with N1 disease and tumour located partly or completely in the central or medial quadrant of the breast.

Axillary Lymph nodes (CTVn_L1, CTVn_L2, CTVn_L3 and CTVn_Interpectoralis): These will be included only if the patients with axillary nodal involvement (cN1-N3) disease are not planned for axillary nodal dissection after NACT. In such a scenario, all three levels will be included. Delineation of the Interpectoral lymph nodes (CTVn_Interpectoralis) is not required unless there was involvement of the same.

sec.title: Delineation of target volume
sec.p: Breast (CTVp_Breast)

Entire breast as defined by a wire marker placed around the breast tissue which is defined at the time of simulation using visual inspection and palpation. In case treatment is planned using forward planning, a CTV will not be delineated for the breast. Field limits will be based on a combination of visual and anatomical landmarks whilst taking into account the volume of organs at risk included in the fields. Intended field limits for patients who have undergone breast conservation are as follows:

list-item.p: Superior: 1 cm above the superior border of the palpable breast tissue.
Inferior: 1 cm below the palpable breast tissue.
Medial: 1 cm medial to the palpable breast tissue at- or ipsilateral to the midline
Lateral: 1 cm lateral to the palpable breast, at or anterior to the mid-axillary line.
Anterior: Adequate margin on the skin (at least 2 cm anterior to the breast contour).

sec.p: If inverse planning is required then the target volume will be delineated as per the ESTRO target volume delineation guidelines (version 1.1, 2016) [28]:

list-item.p: Superior: Upper border of palpable/visible breast tissue maximally up to the sternoclavicular joint.
Inferior: Most caudal CT slice with visible breast.
Medial: Lateral to the medial perforating mammary vessels. Maximum up to the edge of the sternum.
Lateral: Lateral breast fold including the breast parenchyma. Anterior to the lateral thoracic artery
Anterior: 5 mm below skin surface
Posterior: Pectoralis major muscle. Inferiorly where pectoralis major is not visible, the ribs and intercostal muscles will be posterior border

sec.p: Chest wall (CTVp_Chestwall)
Chest wall as defined by wire markers placed at the time of simulation encompassing the scar. The intended field limits for the chest wall is as follows:

list-item.p: Superior: 1 cm above the palpable breast tissue as defined by the contralateral breast
Inferior: 1 cm below the contralateral inframammary fold
Medial: If the scar encroaches into the skin over the sternum then the medial border could be 1 cm beyond the scar and may be beyond the midline. To be discussed during planning.

Lateral: 1 cm postero-lateral to the lateral extent of the scar at or anterior to the mid-axillary line. The lateral extent is to be tailored based upon the included lung and heart volume. If the scar extends beyond the mid-axillary line then it should be discussed.

sec.p: For patients undergoing bilateral mastectomy, the clinical markup should be done by the radiation oncologist.
If inverse planning is required then the following anatomical limits will be delineated as the chest wall ([28]). Coverage of the scar should follow the same principles as outlined above.

list-item.p: Superior: Guided by the contralateral breast tissue as well as visible/palpable signs. Maximally up to the caudal edge of the sternoclavicular joint.
Inferior: As per the contralateral inframammary fold. If bilateral mastectomy has been done then the lower limit is delineated by a wire based on landmarks decided by the physician.
Medial: Guided by the contralateral breast.
Lateral: Guided by the contralateral breast and restricted anterior to the mid-axillary line.
Anterior: 5 mm under the skin surface ensuring the delineated segment does not get discontinuous.
Posterior: Pectoralis major muscle (unless there is involvement of the chest wall) and inferiorly anterior to the ribs and costal cartilages.

sec.p: Residual gross tumour (GTVp)
In patients receiving neoadjuvant radiotherapy, the residual gross tumour will be delineated. The residual gross disease will be delineated using the pre-chemotherapy imaging and clinical findings.
Tumour bed

This will be delineated for patients undergoing adjuvant radiotherapy following breast conservation surgery. The tumour bed will be delineated using the surgical clips placed at the time of breast conservation surgery.
Supraclavicular fossa (CTVn_L4)
For patients undergoing forward planning, the field limits for this volume will be as follows:

list-item.p: Superior: At the level of cricoid or 3 cm above the medial end of the clavicle.

sec.title: Planning target volume (PTV)
sec.p: No specific planning is required for forward planned technique where the fields are designed to account for setup inaccuracy. For inverse planned techniques, use of a PTV is recommended. The margin of PTV to be used will depend on the institutional setup protocol and setup uncertainties. This should be specified in the process document. In case daily image guidance and online correction is used, a 5-mm isotropic margin is recommended.

A boost target volume (BTV) will be generated by an isotropic expansion of 5 mm from the GTVp (in patients receiving neoadjuvant radiotherapy) and the tumour bed (in patients receiving adjuvant radiotherapy after breast conservation surgery).
In all cases it is recommended that PTV margins (including BTV) is trimmed from the skin by 3 mm to ensure dose dumping is not seen when inverse planning techniques are used.

sec.title: Organs at risk
sec.p: The following critical structures will be delineated for each patient:

list-item.p: Lung: Both lungs will be segmented as separate structures using Lung auto segmentation available in most commercial treatment planning systems. Any extra contour extending into trachea or other air cavities should be erased manually after auto segmentation.

Heart: The entire heart will be delineated as a single structure extending from the level of the level of the diaphragm to just inferior to the left pulmonary artery. The entire pericardium should be included in the contour.
Opposite breast: In all patients undergoing a simultaneous integrated boost, the opposite breast will be delineated as a single structure following the guidelines provided by Offersen et al.

The following two structures are optional and may be delineated:
Brachial plexus: All patients in whom regional nodal irradiation is planned, the brachial plexus may be delineated. This will be delineated as per the guidelines proposed by RTOG [29].
Left anterior descending artery: The left anterior descending artery may be delineated as a single solid structure following the guidelines provided by [30] in patients undergoing radiotherapy for left breast cancers.

sec.title: Dose fractionation
sec.p: The following dose fractionation will be used for the study:

list-item.p: Control arm (adjuvant RT 3 weeks radiation): 40 Gy in 15 fractions over 3 weeks to the whole breast or chest wall along with any regional nodes as indicated. Patients undergoing breast conservation therapy will receive additional boost radiotherapy to the tumour bed. This boost will be in the form of a simultaneous integrated boost of 8 Gy (0.53 Gy per day) in 15 fractions. If a sequential boost is used then a dose of 12 Gy in 4 fractions will be used.

Experimental arm 1 (adjuvant RT 1 week radiation): 26 Gy in 5 fractions over 1 week to the whole breast or chest wall along with regional nodes. Treatment volumes will be the same as the control arm. Additional boost will be delivered to patients who have undergone breast conservation. This boost will be in the form of a simultaneous integrated boost of 6 Gy (1.2 Gy per day) in 5 fractions. If a sequential boost is used then a dose of 12 Gy in 4 fractions will be used.

Experimental arm 2 (neoadjuvant RT 3 weeks radiation): 40 Gy in 15 fractions over 3 weeks to the whole breast along with any regional nodes as indicated. An additional boost to residual disease will be administered. This boost will be in the form of a simultaneous integrated boost of 8 Gy (0.53 Gy per day) in 15 fractions. If a sequential boost is used, then a dose of 12 Gy in 4 fractions will be used.

Experimental arm 3 (neoadjuvant RT 1 weeks radiation): 26 Gy in 5 fractions over 1 week to the whole breast along with any regional nodes as indicated. An additional boost to residual disease will be administered. This boost will be in the form of a simultaneous integrated boost of 6 Gy (1.2 Gy per day) in 5 fractions. If a sequential boost is used then a dose of 12 Gy in 4 fractions will be used.

sec.title: Dose specification
sec.p: The radiation dose for the whole breast or chest wall plan will be prescribed to a reference point within the breast or the chest wall. For patients requiring supraclavicular fossa irradiation, the dose will be specified to the depth of maximum dose (Dmax). For patients treated with inverse planned intensity modulated radiotherapy, no additional plan normalisation will be performed. For the patients receiving a simultaneous integrated boost the plan will be prescribed to the same reference point as that of the tangential plan, such that the plan sum of the tangential and boost plans ensures coverage of the boost target volume by at least 95% of the prescribed dose. All fields will be treated on all days during the treatments. Treatment will be delivered once daily, 5 days a week over 5 weeks. The total dose prescribed will be as given in the following table.

In case sequential boost is utilised, the prescribed dose will be 12 Gy in 4 fractions (over 4 days) in both arms. Prescription point will be the reference point or if an electron boost is used to 100% isodose. A tangential field in field forward planned intensity modulated radiotherapy (IMRT) technique or enface electrons will be used for this boost.

sec.title: Treatment planning
sec.p: A standard treatment planning technique should be adopted which should be pre-specified in the process document for each centre. Both field-based planning and inverse planning done after target volume delineation are allowed in the protocol based on the process document. Irrespective of the technique adopted for the treatment planning, doses to the organs at risk should be respected.

The planned dose should be prescribed to a point in the target volume or a volume. If a point-based prescription technique is followed, then the International Commission on Radiation Units and Measurements (ICRU) recommendations for dose reporting should be followed for plan evaluation. In the case of volumetric prescription, the ICRU 84 recommendations should be followed.

Both field-based planning and target volume-based planning are allowed in this study and institutes should prespecify the technique to be used for this study. During site commissioning the central trial coordinating committee will evaluate at least 5 treatment plans which have been planned following the technique to be commissioned. Use of physical wedges, field-in-field forward planned IMRT, dynamic or virtual wedges is allowed for dose homogenisation for tangential irradiation but the choice(s) of the technique to be used should be specified. Use of inverse planned techniques is allowed in the trial if appropriate target volume coverage would need the same.

Treatment planning should involve dose calculation using an algorithm that incorporates heterogeneity correction for accurate estimation of the lung dose. The dose calculation grid should not be coarser than 5 mm. The calculated dose distribution should be visualised on the treatment planning system as isodose overlays as well as dose volume histograms for plan evaluation.

sec.p: Bolus should not be used in patients undergoing breast conservation or those who are undergoing neoadjuvant radiotherapy.

sec.title: Beam energy
sec.p: Beam energies should be used as per the local policy and most patients will be planned with 6 MV photons. However, higher energy beams will be allowed in order to achieve appropriate coverage of the breast and tumour bed. If higher energy beams will be used on a regular basis then the same should be pre-specified by the institution.

sec.title: Treatment delivery
sec.p: Radiotherapy will be delivered using megavoltage equipment on 5 days a week treating one fraction per day. All fields should be treated on all days. Verification imaging will be performed prior to delivery of all fractions. Patients with left-sided breast cancer will preferably be treated using Deep Inspiration Breath Hold (DIBH).

sec.title: Verification
sec.p: Verification of the treatment plan would include a planar or volumetric on-board image obtained prior to the first fraction of treatment. Planar imaging may be performed using Megavoltage (MV) Electronic portal images (EPID) or Kilovoltage (KV) X-rays. At least a pair of orthogonal images should be obtained for all patients. A mix of MV and KV images is allowed. If facilities are commissioned, then volumetric cone beam CT images should be obtained as per the departmental protocol to allow volumetric imaging. The volumetric imaging performed should have specified parameters but at a minimum should include the ipsilateral breast and a craniocaudal length of 15 cm. Cine mode imaging could be preferably acquired at the time of treatment delivery as per institutional policy.

For patients undergoing simultaneous integrated boost to the boost target volume, it is important to ensure that the setup errors are minimised; hence, cone beam imaging should be performed in all these patients. Ideally, patients should undergo daily imaging. If this is not feasible then the protocol of CBCT imaging and matching should be specified in the process document. The first 3 imaging should be reviewed to ensure that errors in the setup at the level Boost target volume are within the threshold of the margins used around the tumour bed. Daily CBCT will be preferred and if not feasible a No action level (NAL) protocol should be applied. At least one CBCT imaging should be obtained per week for 3-week radiotherapy. For patients receiving 5 fraction regimen, CBCT imaging should be performed on at least 4 of the 5 treatments.

sec.title: Cone beam CT scan
sec.p: Patients undergoing SIB should undergo cone beam CT prior to each fraction. CBCTs will be obtained with half fan, using 125 kV, and 25 ms/frame. Axial images of the breast will be acquired. After the acquisition, automatic rigid registration in the three cardinal axes will be performed with a volume of interest placed 0.5 cm around the clips outlining the tumour bed.

sec.title: On treatment reviews
sec.p: On treatment, reviews will be performed at weekly intervals for all patients. During each review visit, patients would be examined clinically to document any toxicities especially cutaneous and mucosal toxicities. Toxicity grading will be done using the Common Terminology Criteria of Adverse Events (CTCAE) version 5.00. Please refer to Appendix II for the CTCAE terms and definitions to be used for various toxicities.

sec.title: Treatment scheduling and gaps
sec.p: Treatments can start on any day of the week. A gap of 3 days is acceptable in case of machine breakdown. This is preferable to transferring to a machine in which daily image guidance capabilities are not available. In case of longer gaps or interruptions, dose per fraction should not be adjusted. Treatment on Saturdays to compensate for longer delays (> 3 days) is acceptable.

sec.title: Radiotherapy Quality Assurance (RTQA)
sec.p: A comprehensive quality assurance is planned for all centres participating in this trial and the same has been detailed in the RTQA pack.

sec.title: Criteria for discontinuing or modifying allocated interventions {11b}
sec.p: Breast cancer radiotherapy is not expected to result in substantial adverse effects. Treatment should not be interrupted unless the patient has a Grade III-IV CTCAE adverse event. Any and all such events should be reported. After this treatment can be restarted once the toxicity has reduced to Grade I or less and if in the treating physician’s opinion it is safe to continue with treatment.

sec.title: Strategies to improve adherence to interventions {11c}
sec.p: Weekly reviews during radiotherapy will be undertaken to ensure adherence to the radiotherapy treatment protocol.

The use of endocrine therapy in the neoadjuvant setting after neoadjuvant chemotherapy is not recommended as it is not a current standard of practice.

Patients receiving adjuvant or neoadjuvant radiotherapy may receive concurrent topical steroids to reduce the incidence of radiation dermatitis [31, 32]. Additional medications may be given for radiation-related nausea, vomiting, and analgesics for pain in the breast/chest wall as appropriate.

sec.title: Provisions for post-trial care {30}
sec.p: Patients will continue to receive post trial care as per the institutional protocols in place. Ancillary care for late toxicity-related outcomes will also be provided as per the standard institutional protocol. Patients enrolled will be covered by indemnity for negligent harm through an insurance policy for the trial. Additional coverage for additional healthcare, compensation and damages will also be covered through the same insurance policy.

sec.title: Primary outcome
sec.p: The primary outcome of interest is the invasive disease-free survival (iDFS) at 3 years. Invasive disease-free survival is a composite endpoint which comprises of any recurrence (local recurrence/regional recurrence/distant metastases), development of ipsilateral or contralateral invasive breast cancer or ductal carcinoma in situ, any invasive second malignancy or death due to any cause [33]. The event of interest is the first event that occurs for each patient and the interval between the date of randomisation to the date of occurrence of the first event will be used for calculating disease-free survival. The proportion of patients who are disease free at 3 years will be calculated. Comparison of iDFS of patients receiving adjuvant radiotherapy versus neoadjuvant radiotherapy will be presented.

Invasive disease-free survival is a composite endpoint of interest in this trial as the impact of neoadjuvant radiotherapy may be observed in both loco-regional recurrence as well as distant metastases. Invasive disease-free survival also has a high degree of correlation with overall survival at individual patient level and at a trial level as demonstrated by a recent meta-analysis by Savina et al. [34].

sec.title: Breast induration
sec.p: The key secondary endpoint of interest is to compare the proportion of patients with patient reported moderate to marked breast or chest wall induration (in or outside the tumour bed) in the ipsilateral breast during follow-up between the two fractionation schedules. This endpoint has been selected as it can be assessed in both patients undergoing mastectomy as well as breast conservation surgery. Additionally, this endpoint was different between the two arms in the FAST-Forward trial [16] and therefore would be an indicator of the difference in the late normal tissue effects between the two fractionation schedules. Proportion of patients with moderate to marked breast or chest wall induration at any point of time during follow-up will be compared between the two dose fractionation schedules.

sec.title: Additional cancer-related outcomes
sec.p: Additional cancer-related outcomes of interest which will be compared between the two treatment sequences (neoadjuvant versus adjuvant) include:

list-item.p: Locoregional recurrence at 3 years which will be reported as the cumulative incidence of any recurrence in the ipsilateral breast, chest wall or regional lymph nodes (axilla, supraclavicular fossa and internal mammary nodes).
Breast cancer-specific survival at 3 years which will be calculated as the time interval between randomisation and death related to breast cancer
Overall survival at 3 years which will be calculated as the time interval between randomisation and death due to any cause.

sec.title: Clinician-reported late normal tissue effects
sec.p: The proportion of patients with any clinician reported moderate to marked late locoregional (breast/chest wall/arm) late normal tissue effects will be compared between the two arms. The following will be the events of interest:

list-item.p: Breast distortion (only in patients with breast conservation)
Breast shrinkage (only in patients with breast conservation)
Breast induration in tumour bed (only in patients undergoing breast conservation)
Breast induration outside tumour bed (only in patients undergoing breast conservation)
Telangiectasia (both patients undergoing breast conservation and mastectomy)
Breast or chest wall edema (both patients undergoing breast conservation and mastectomy)
Breast or chest wall discomfort (both patients undergoing breast conservation and mastectomy
Lymphedema of the upper extremity (both patients undergoing breast conservation and mastectomy)

sec.p: In addition to reporting the proportion of patients with any of the late normal tissue effects, the proportion of patients experiencing the individual effects will also be compared between the two treatment sequences (neoadjuvant versus adjuvant).

sec.title: Patient-reported outcomes
sec.p: Patient-reported outcomes will be compared between the two treatment sequences (neoadjuvant versus adjuvant). Patient-reported outcomes will be obtained using the European Organization for Research and Treatment of Cancer (EORTC) core quality of life questionnaire (EORTC QLQ C30) and the EORTC Breast cancer module (EORTC BR 45) questionnaires [35]. Mean scores of the derived functional and symptom scales from both the questionnaires will be compared across the two treatment sequences (neoadjuvant versus adjuvant).

sec.title: Clinician-reported toxicity
sec.p: Clinician-reported toxicity will be captured using the CTCAE scale as used in the HYPORT Adjuvant trial. Maximum grades of clinician-reported adverse events will be compared between the two treatment sequences (NART vs ART).

sec.title: Substudy I: Perforator substudy
sec.p: The primary outcome of interest for the substudy is the detection of patent chest wall perforators among patients receiving NART. Detection of patency will be performed using a handheld Doppler ultrasound performed by a trained breast surgeon. The patency of the perforators will be ascertained at predefined locations along the inframammary crease and along the anterior axillary line. These perforator vessels are used to decide the suitability of the chest wall perforator flap to be used for reconstruction.

sec.title: Substudy II: Sentinel lymph node detection substudy
sec.p: The sentinel lymph node detection substudy will be performed in patients who will undergo planned sentinel lymph node biopsy after neoadjuvant chemotherapy. The outcome of interest is the proportion of patients for whom sentinel lymph nodes are not detected when the surgery is done (also known as detection rate).

sec.title: Substudy III: Pathological complete response
sec.p: The change in pathological complete response rate due to use of neoadjuvant radiotherapy will be reported in the second interim analysis. For this analysis, the pathological complete response rates will be compared between patients undergoing neoadjuvant radiotherapy and those undergoing upfront surgery. The definition of pathological complete response will be based upon the current institutional practice. Patients will be considered to have a pathological complete response if there is absence of residual invasive cancer on Haematoxylin and Eosin evaluation of the complete resected breast specimen and all sample regional nodes (ypT0/ypTis) [36]. It is important that the specimens are processed as per the standard recommendation for this to be accurate.
The residual cancer burden (RCB) would also be recorded as per the CAP guidelines [37]. The RCB score will also be compared between the patients undergoing NART vs ART.

sec.title: Substudy IV: Wound complication rates
sec.p: Safety of preoperative radiotherapy in terms of wound complication will be assessed. Wound complication rates following neoadjuvant radiotherapy will be reported as part of the first interim analysis. Major wound complications as defined on the Calvien Dindo rating system would be considered as significant. We would be estimating the proportion of patients developing grade III–V wound complications till 12 weeks after surgery. As per the scale, Grade III complications are those which represent surgical, endoscopic and radiological intervention (III a without and IIIb with general anaesthesia). Grade IV complications are those which result in life threatening complications with ICU admission and grade V complications result in death of the patient [38].

sec.title: Participant timelines {13}
sec.p: Participants will be screened in the trial when they are planned for neoadjuvant chemotherapy (Fig. 2). Additional screening investigations are not required for the trial. Randomisation will be performed after completion of neoadjuvant chemotherapy. Eligibility checklist should be completed and written informed consent should be obtained prior to randomisation. Patients will be randomised centrally and allocated into one of the four arms of the trial.

sec.p: Baseline assessments will include a history and physical examination, documentation of the clinician-reported baseline normal tissue status and assessment of patient-reported outcomes using the EORTC QLQ C30 and BR45 questionnaires. Additionally, surgical decision for breast conservation or mastectomy as well as axillary staging procedures planned will be documented in all arms.

Participants enrolled in the neoadjuvant radiotherapy arms will undergo neoadjuvant radiotherapy followed by surgery 4 to 6 weeks after completion of radiotherapy. Patients in the adjuvant therapy arms will undergo surgery first followed by adjuvant radiotherapy. Patient-reported outcomes will also be obtained at the end of radiotherapy from all participants.
For the initial 70 patients enrolled in the neoadjuvant radiotherapy arm, wound complication will be documented at 6 weeks after surgery as a part of substudy I.

Patients undergoing adjuvant radiotherapy will be reviewed 6 weeks after completion of radiotherapy whilst patients undergoing neoadjuvant radiotherapy will be reviewed 6 weeks after completion of surgery. After this the patients will be reviewed at 6 monthly intervals till 12 months (2 visits) and then annually till two more years (years 2 and 3). Assessments will include physical examination, documentation of the late normal tissue effects, wound complications and patient-reported outcomes. Patient-reported outcomes may also be recorded at any interim visits that occur in between the scheduled visits after 6 weeks.
